questions.text:
Mānuka leaves contain a range of bioactive molecules, including leptospermone, which contributes to their distinctive aroma. Another compound isolated from mānuka oil is grandiflorone.

The molecule grandiflorone contains two key functional groups, labelled A and B.

Group A has the structure: R-C=C-R (a carbon-to-carbon double bond)
Group B has the structure: R-O-H (a hydroxyl group attached to a carbon)

Name the functional groups labelled A and B:
A:
B:
questions.expectedAnswer: A: Alkene / carbon-to-carbon double bond. B: (Primary) alcohol / hydroxyl.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct identification of both groups.

questions.text:
Identification tests were carried out to confirm the presence of groups A and B in the molecule.

Name the reagents and any conditions required for identifying group A and group B separately.

Reagents/Conditions:
A:

questions.expectedAnswer: A: Bromine water (Br2(aq)) — decolourises from orange/brown to colourless. B: Acidified permanganate (MnO4-/H+) or acidified dichromate (Cr2O72-/H+) with heating.

questions.text:
Describe the observation that would occur in a positive test for each group. Include:
- the reaction type
- the name of the functional group of the product
- a drawing of the functional group of the product.

A:

questions.expectedAnswer: A: Bromine water decolourises from orange to colourless. Reaction type: addition. Product functional group: haloalkane (dihaloalkane, two C-Br bonds). B: Acidified purple permanganate becomes colourless OR acidified orange dichromate becomes green. Reaction type: oxidation. Product functional group: carboxylic acid (-COOH).

questions.text:
When preparing extracts from native plants, researchers often use different solvents including pentan-1-ol, ethanol, and heptane. All three solvents are colourless liquids at room temperature.

Explain the procedure you could use to distinguish between pentan-1-ol, ethanol, and heptane, based solely on their physical properties.

Give reasons for the different results between solvents.

Physical properties are limited to differences in melting point, boiling point, and solubility in water.
questions.expectedAnswer: Mix each unknown solvent in a test tube with water. Heptane (alkane) is non-polar and immiscible with water, forming a separate layer. Ethanol is miscible with water and pentan-1-ol is only partially miscible, as their polar hydroxyl groups can form hydrogen bonds with water. Distinguish ethanol from pentan-1-ol by measuring boiling points: ethanol boils at about 78 degrees C, pentan-1-ol at about 138 degrees C, because pentan-1-ol has a longer carbon chain producing stronger London dispersion forces.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies ethanol or pentan-1-ol as miscible/soluble OR identifies heptane as an alkane. Merit: Correctly identifies heptane as non-soluble AND provides method to distinguish between the two alcohols. Excellence: Explains how all three can be distinguished, with reference to solubility, molecular structure, and carbon chain effects.

questions.text:
Polypropylene (PP) is widely used in packaging for bags, bottles, and wrapping. PP is an addition polymer made from the propene monomer.

The monomer propene has the structure: H2C=CH-CH3

In the box below, draw three repeating units of the PP polymer.
questions.expectedAnswer: Three repeating units showing the C-C backbone with a methyl branch on alternating carbons: -[CH2-CH(CH3)]3-
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies polymer is orientated correctly (C-C saturated backbone). Merit: Labels saturated (C-C) or monomer is unsaturated (C=C).

questions.text:
Plastics made from PP are durable and resistant to chemical attack.

Explain why the monomer propene is more reactive than the polymer PP.

In your answer you should:
- explain the term 'addition polymerisation'
- explain the difference in structure, and link it to chemical reactivity
- relate how this difference is important for the uses of the polymer.
questions.expectedAnswer: In an addition polymerisation reaction, C=C double bonds in the monomer are broken and reform as single C-C bonds, linking many monomer units into a long chain. The monomer is more reactive because the C=C double bond is a region of high electron density, making it susceptible to electrophilic addition reactions. The polymer has only single C-C bonds, which are much less reactive. This chemical stability is essential for PP's uses in packaging materials that must resist degradation.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies polymer is orientated correctly OR partial explanation of addition polymerisation. Merit: Links saturated/unsaturated nature of polymer/monomer to materials reactivity AND explains addition polymerisation. Excellence: Explains the difference of monomer and polymer in terms of structure, reactivity and use.

questions.text:
An incomplete reaction scheme starting with 2-bromopentane, Compound A, is shown.

Compound A (2-bromopentane) undergoes Reaction type W with Reagent 1 to form Compound B (an alkene) and Compound C (a different alkene isomer). Compound B reacts with H2O/H+ and heat to form Compound D (an alcohol). Compound B also forms Compound E (a secondary alcohol on C2 of pentane). Compound C reacts with MnO4-/H+ in Reaction type X to form Compound F. Compound F reacts with Cr2O72-/H+ and heat to form Compound H. Compound H reacts with KOH in Reaction type Z to form Compound J (a potassium salt of a carboxylic acid).

(i) Draw the structural formulae of Compounds C, D, E, and H.
(ii) Complete the Reagents 1 and 2.
questions.expectedAnswer: Compound C: pent-1-ene (H2C=CH-CH2-CH2-CH3). Compound D: pentan-2-ol (Markovnikov addition of H2O to pent-2-ene) or pentan-1-ol / pentan-2-ol from pent-1-ene. Compound E: pentan-2-ol. Compound H: pentanoic acid. Reagent 1: KOH(alc)/heat (elimination). Reagent 2: H2O/H+.

questions.text:
The starting material Compound A, 2-bromopentane, is a secondary haloalkane.

Draw the tertiary isomer of chlorobutane and explain why it is classified as tertiary.
questions.expectedAnswer: Structure: 2-chloro-2-methylpropane, i.e. (CH3)3CCl. This is a tertiary haloalkane because the carbon bonded to the chlorine is also bonded to three other carbon atoms (no hydrogen atoms on the C bearing Cl).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct structure OR explanation. Merit: Correct structure AND explanation.

questions.text:
When Compound B (pent-1-ene) reacts with hydrogen chloride, HCl, without heat, two products are formed in differing amounts.

Compound B: H2C=CH-CH2-CH2-CH3 (pent-1-ene)

Discuss the reaction of Compound B with hydrogen chloride.
In your answer you should:
- name and explain this type of reaction
- draw the structures of both products, in the appropriate box for the major and minor products
- justify your choice of major and minor products.
questions.expectedAnswer: This is an addition reaction. The HCl adds across the C=C double bond. According to Markovnikov's rule, the H adds to the carbon with more H atoms (C1 of pent-1-ene, which has 2 H), and the Cl adds to the more substituted carbon (C2, which has 1 H). Major product: 2-chloropentane (Cl on C2). Minor product: 1-chloropentane (Cl on C1).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct structure for one product OR identifies the haloalkane is formed. Merit: Explains major/minor and identifies both structures. Excellence: Explanation of addition reaction, options for major/minor products, and why they are produced in this situation.

questions.text:
Compare the reaction of Compound B with bromine, Br2, against the previous reaction of Compound B with HCl.

In your answer you should:
- explain why a different number of products are formed in the same type of reaction
- draw any relevant product structures.
questions.expectedAnswer: With Br2, both atoms that add across the double bond are the same (both Br), so both possible orientations give the same product: 1,2-dibromopentane. There is only ONE product, not two. With HCl, the two atoms (H and Cl) are different, so which atom ends up on which carbon matters, producing two different products (major and minor). The symmetry of the Br2 molecule means Markovnikov's rule does not apply.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies symmetry as a factor OR identifies both structures are the same. Merit: Links symmetry and asymmetry of reactions. Excellence: Full explanation including why only one product for Br2 and two for HCl.

Describe a two-step series of reactions to convert Compound M (heptan-3-ol) into Compound P (hept-3-ene, a straight-chain alkene).

Step 1 starts with Compound M:
Reaction type:
Reagents and any conditions:
Products' functional group:
Draw the structure of ALL products.

Step 2 ends with Compound P:
Reaction type:
Reagents and any conditions:
questions.expectedAnswer: Step 1: Substitution — react heptan-3-ol with concentrated HBr (or HCl) to convert the alcohol into 3-bromoheptane (a secondary haloalkane). Product functional group: haloalkane. Step 2: Elimination — heat 3-bromoheptane with KOH(alc) to give hept-2-ene and hept-3-ene (the hept-3-ene is the required alkene product).

questions.text:
The elimination reaction in Step 1 produces two isomers with the same functional group in equal quantities.

Explain why there is no major or minor product of the hydrocarbon produced.

In your answer you should explain:
- the type of reaction
- what determines major and minor products
- why the products are equal in this situation.
questions.expectedAnswer: An elimination reaction results in the formation of a C=C double bond by removing a small molecule (HBr when using KOH(alc) with a haloalkane). When the Br (or OH) is on C3 of heptane, the double bond can form between C2-C3 (hept-2-ene) or C3-C4 (hept-3-ene). Because C2 and C4 each carry the same number of hydrogen atoms available for elimination, the products form in approximately equal amounts — there is an equal probability of H being removed from either adjacent carbon, so neither alkene is favoured as the major product.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Partial explanation of an elimination reaction OR states that in an elimination reaction a double bond could form in either direction. Merit: Explains what determines major/minor products. Excellence: Explanation of elimination reaction, options for products, what determines a majority/minority and why they are produced in equal amounts for this situation.

questions.text:
Compounds Q and R below each contain a carbon-to-carbon double bond, but only one of them can form geometric isomers.

HO-CH2-CH=CH-CH2-CH2-CH3     HO-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH=CH2
     Compound Q                    Compound R

Which compound forms geometric isomers?
questions.expectedAnswer: Compound Q will form geometric isomers.

questions.text: Draw the cis and trans geometric isomers of the compound you identified, and label each correctly.
questions.expectedAnswer: Trans isomer: HOCH2 and CH2CH2CH3 on opposite sides of the C=C double bond. Cis isomer: HOCH2 and CH2CH2CH3 on the same side of the C=C double bond.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct compound and isomers identified. Merit: Both structures correct with correct cis/trans labels.
